title: Nietzsche's Eternal Return
objective: After this level you can explain Nietzsche's test of living your life again forever and why he thought saying yes to it mattered after "God is dead".
summary: After diagnosing that “God is dead”, Nietzsche’s demon tests whether you can affirm this life as it is, forever. Readers dispute whether it is a test or a claim about time.

cards.headline: What if you had to live this exact life again, forever?
cards.body: Every joy and every pain, in the same order, with nothing new. Friedrich Nietzsche turned that nightmare, or dream, into a test.

cards.headline: “God is dead”
cards.body: In The Gay Science (1882), a madman announces that “God is dead”. He brings the news to people who already don’t believe, so Nietzsche’s point isn’t simply that atheism is true. It’s a diagnosis of a culture: belief in the Christian God had become unbelievable, so everything built on it, including Europe’s morality, was bound to collapse. What could give life value then?

cards.headline: The demon’s offer
cards.body: Near the end of the same book, a demon finds you in your loneliest loneliness. You must live this life again, innumerable times, “this spider and this moonlight among the trees” included. Would you gnash your teeth and curse him? Or answer, “Thou art a God, and never did I hear aught more divine!”? That question, Nietzsche wrote, would lie on every act as “the heaviest burden”.

cards.headline: Why the yes matters
cards.body: Many readers treat it as a thought experiment: your gut reaction shows how you really value your life, like being asked whether you’d marry your spouse again. On one reading it also blocks an escape. No later reward can redeem a life that returns forever, so the yes has to be to this life, as it is. Nietzsche’s name for that love was amor fati, love of fate.

cards.headline: Or a claim about time?
cards.body: Early readers took the return literally, as a theory that all events repeat in endless cycles, and critics raised problems for it read that way. Some scholars, such as Paul Loeb, still defend that reading. So even the idea’s basic status, test or theory, is contested.

cards.headline: Nietzsche’s Eternal Return: the big picture
learned: The demon: live this life again, forever
The test asks for a yes to life as it is
Test or theory of time? Still debated

questions.prompt: In The Gay Science, what does Nietzsche’s demon tell you?

options.label: That you will be rewarded for this life in another world later
That you may change one thing about your past
That you must live this same life again, innumerable times
That your life will soon be forgotten
options.rationale: The demon promises return, not oblivion.

questions.explanation: The demon says you must live this life again innumerable times, with nothing new in it.

questions.prompt: Match each figure or phrase with what it stands for in Nietzsche.
questions.explanation: A madman announces that God is dead, the demon says you must live this life again, and amor fati means love of fate.

questions.prompt: Early readers took the eternal return as a claim that all events literally repeat in cycles, a claim that belongs to the branch of philosophy called _____.

options.label: ethics
options.rationale: A claim about how the universe runs isn’t about right and wrong.

questions.explanation: Claims about what exists and how the world is structured, such as time repeating, belong to metaphysics.
